name: Test-only cycle

lead: A test-only cycle means a course of testosterone as the only anabolic steroid, without other compounds added. In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles it is often called the baseline or beginner approach, aimed at more muscle, a fuller physique and, in some posts, secondary effects on the face.

Testosterone activates androgen receptors and promotes muscle growth and maintenance. Forum users disagree about its appearance trade-offs, with some calling it all that is needed and others arguing it brings aging, hair-loss and skin effects.

paras: Users describe it in general terms as an injected testosterone ester taken for a number of weeks, sometimes paired with hair-loss or other support products. Dosing and sourcing are not covered here.

Documented effects include acne, oily skin, scalp hair loss in predisposed people, suppression of natural testosterone and sperm production, raised blood pressure and unfavourable cholesterol changes, and cardiovascular concerns. Testosterone is a controlled substance (US Schedule III, UK Class C) and is on the WADA prohibited list.

angle.text: Testosterone raises androgen levels, which promotes muscle growth and maintenance. Users use a test-only course to build a bigger physique, while discussing trade-offs in hair, skin and face.

lead: A test-only cycle is a period of non-medical testosterone use in which no other anabolic-androgenic steroid is added, as opposed to "stacking" several compounds. Among people who train for physique it is described as the baseline or beginner approach, and users pursue it for more muscle, a fuller and more V-shaped upper body, leaner-looking composition and, in some posts, effects on the face and skin.[1][2][3]

Testosterone is the reference androgen: through androgen receptor activation it supports muscle growth and maintenance, and it also acts on skin, hair, red blood cells and fertility.[4][5] Injectable esters are the usual non-medical route because oral testosterone is largely inactivated before reaching the circulation.[5]

The research base for the muscle effect is substantial. A 1996 randomised trial in 43 healthy men found that supraphysiologic testosterone increased muscle size and strength, most of all when combined with strength training,[6] and a 2001 dose-response study found that fat-free mass and muscle volume rose in step with testosterone level.[6] An Endocrine Society scientific statement describes the adverse effects associated with non-medical androgen use and notes that most users are non-athlete weightlifters.[7]

On looksmax.org the topic is contested. One thread titled "All you need is a test only cycle" presents it as a sufficient route to an above-natural-limit physique, while another argues testosterone is "unselective" and produces ageing, hair and skin effects for modest muscle; others ask whether it helps facial bone mass or causes hair loss.[1][2][3][8]
infobox: Intramuscular injection of esters is the usual non-medical route[5]
US Schedule III, UK Class C, Canada Schedule IV[4]
Mostly non-athlete weightlifters, median starting age about 22-24[7]

paras: The term describes testosterone used on its own rather than combined with other steroids. Testosterone esters act as prodrugs that release the hormone over time, and intramuscular injection is the most common route.[4] "Cycle" refers to a defined period of use followed by a break; the wiki does not cover doses, durations or sourcing.

Users often frame the test-only approach as the least complicated option: one compound, with the body's own testosterone as the reference point. Posts describe it as a way to exceed a "natty limit" (the muscle a person can build without drugs) in less time than years of training.[3]

Testosterone was isolated in 1935 and approved for medical use in 1939 for hypogonadism.[5] Synthetic anabolic steroids spread through bodybuilding and sport in the following decades, and the United States designated them controlled substances in 1990.[5]

Non-medical users today are mostly not competitive athletes. The Endocrine Society statement states that the vast majority of performance-enhancing drug users are non-athlete weightlifters, estimates at least 3 million users in the US, and reports median age of first use of 22 to 24.[7] Wikipedia reports that a survey found about 78 percent of users were noncompetitive bodybuilders or non-athletes who use for cosmetic reasons.[4]

Looksmaxxing writers distinguish 'softmaxxing' (skincare, grooming, fitness) from 'hardmaxxing', which Wikipedia lists as including anabolic steroids, growth hormone, peptides and aromatase inhibitors.[9] Testosterone use is discussed within this wider culture of physique and face optimisation.

Posters on looksmax.org ask whether a test-only course can build facial bone mass, whether it causes hair loss, and whether it is enough on its own.[1][3][8] Replies range from telling a tall 18-year-old he does not need it to arguing that testosterone is a poor choice for looks and that more tissue-selective compounds are preferable.[1][2]

A pro-test post argues that most other compounds are more metabolically taxing, that a surfer or swimmer physique is attractive enough, and that test alone can deliver an above-natural-limit build.[3] Replies in that thread disagree about the ideal physique, with one naming competitive bodybuilders as the target.[3]
Hair is a recurring theme: another thread notes that hair loss is the main concern users cite and that some pair use with hair-loss medications; the hair question is asked repeatedly.[2][8]

In the 1996 randomised trial, 43 healthy men received weekly testosterone or placebo with or without supervised weight training for 10 weeks. Testosterone without exercise increased muscle size and strength, and testosterone plus exercise produced the largest gains in fat-free mass, muscle size and strength; mood and behaviour did not change.[6]

In the 2001 study, 61 healthy young men had their own testosterone suppressed and were given a range of weekly testosterone enanthate doses for 20 weeks. Fat-free mass, strength, power and muscle volume rose with testosterone concentration along a single linear dose-response relationship, while fat mass and HDL cholesterol fell.[6]
Both studies involved clinical administration in research settings; they did not examine the combinations, durations and conditions of community use, or effects on facial bones.

Reviews list acne, oily skin, stretch marks, fluid retention, accelerated pattern baldness in predisposed men via DHT, suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis with reduced sperm production, gynecomastia, raised LDL and lowered HDL cholesterol, hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy.[4][5] The FDA changed testosterone labelling in February 2025, adding a blood pressure warning.[5]

The Endocrine Society statement reports that suppression of the axis after a lengthy course may last months or years, that some users do not regain normal testosterone, and that about a third of users (32.5 percent in a pooled analysis of 10 studies) develop dependence; it notes that most evidence comes from case reports, surveys and case-control studies rather than prospective trials.[7] Wikipedia notes that a short course followed by clomiphene or hCG usually restores production, a point the statement describes as lacking systematic trials.[4][7]

Clinicians writing about looksmaxxing warn about overdose, addiction and psychological problems with steroid use and recommend screening for it in boys and young men; the Cleveland Clinic and a 2026 Journal of Adolescent Health commentary both raise this.[10][11]

Testosterone is Schedule III in the US, Class C in the UK and Schedule IV in Canada, prescription-only in the EU, and on the WADA list.[4][5] A black market of smuggled or counterfeit products exists in regulated markets.[4]

Looksmaxxing has been covered by Vice, The New York Times, The Guardian, the BBC and others since 2018, with attention in 2026 on influencers and extreme practices.[9] Clinicians quoted in news coverage and the Cleveland Clinic describe anabolic steroids and testosterone among substances some young looksmaxxers use.[10]

No studies found of the "test-only cycle" as practised in these communities. Related research covers supraphysiologic testosterone given to healthy men in controlled settings[6][6] and medical testosterone replacement.[5]

lore.intro: Test-only cycles are widely debated on looksmax.org as a baseline, with disagreement about benefits versus ageing and hair effects.[1][2][3]
